extracted.intended_audience: members and ministers of the Presbyterian Church (Scottish covenanted tradition); readers of a Presbytery's official testimony
extracted.subtask_description: An official Presbytery statement setting out the grounds (theological, scriptural, and historical) on which it testifies against the civil and ecclesiastical constitutions established at the Revolution of 1689, and against related doctrines/practices (popery, prelaty, Erastianism, indulgences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to reintroduction of Popery
rubrics_metrics.description: Protest against the proclamation of James, duke of York (a professed and excommunicated papist) and against 'all kinds of popery, general and particular heads' as abjured by the national covenant; oppose any entry or measures that 'do, or may directly or indirectly, make way' for popery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: royal proclamations and tolerations that permitted Papists to practice openly, conversion of churches to mass chapels, repair of royal chapel for popish service, and influx of Jesuits and priests. The Presbytery treats such toleration as part of a deliberate design to extinguish the gospel and bring in 'Antichrist.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of indulgences/tolerations that favor Papists but persecute faithful Presbyterians
rubrics_metrics.description: The King's proclamations granting 'toleration' (to Presbyterians, Quakers, and Papists) are condemned where they are 'clogged with a number of grievous Erastian conditions' and where, simultaneously, field conventicles and faithful Presbyterians are still prosecuted with rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific historical proclamations are cited (e.g., Feb 12, 1687; June 28, 1687). The Presbytery treats such measures as deceitful: outwardly granting liberty while preserving laws and prosecutions that target true dissenting worship (field meetings), thereby rewarding false conformity and punishing genuine testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of oaths imposing absolute passive and active obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: The oath enjoined by the King's proclamation—requiring absolute subjection, passive obedience (never to resist) and absolute active obedience (to 'assist, defend, and maintain him, his heirs and successors, in the exercise of their absolute power')—is 'palpably gross and odious' and must be disdained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery cites the text of the oath and the practical effect of binding conscience to unlimited royal authority as grounds for refusing such allegiance; ministers and people should not accept oaths that oblige support for arbitrary and absolute power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural requirement for legitimate civil sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil constitution is illegitimate if it places a 'stranger' or one not 'of thy brethren' over the nation; a ruler must be 'just, ruling in the fear of God' (Deut. xvii.15; 2 Sam. xxiii.3). Choosing William and Mary (foreigners by birth and religious training) is therefore contrary to scripture and covenant duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery uses Deuteronomy and 2 Samuel to argue that the Revolution settlement violated scriptural prescriptions about who may lawfully hold the civil scepter and the character required of such rulers. They critique oaths and political choices that allow 'strangers' or those schooled in Erastian views to govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to Erastianism (state supremacy over the church)
rubrics_metrics.description: The presbytery testifies against doctrines and practices that ascribe excessive power to the civil magistrate over the church (Erastianism), including measures that suspend penal laws or otherwise place church governance at the mercy of 'prerogative royal and absolute power.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proclamations that suspend penal laws, require limits on preaching that could 'alienate the hearts of the people from him and his government', and grant the civil magistrate power inconsistent with church autonomy. The Presbytery treats these as 'Christ-dethroning supremacy' and an affront to the covenanted church order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-recognition of usurpation and illegitimate power (e.g., Cromwell)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Presbytery declares against the usurpation of Oliver Cromwell and those who 'subjected themselves unto, and owned, his authority', condemning his invasion, sectarian toleration, and subversion of the covenanted order as contrary to Scripture and national covenants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They cite prior acts and assemblies that warned against receiving malignants into trust and argue that Cromwell's toleration of sects endangered both true religion and civil liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reprobation of the Restoration of Charles II for duplicity and anti-reformation measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The restoration of Charles II is condemned because he showed 'disingenuity' (public resolutions enabling malignants), re-established prelaty (diocesan and Erastian Prelacy), nullified covenants (act rescissory), burned the covenants publicly, and exercised cruelty and persecution against the Lord's people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery traces legal acts (e.g., annulling covenants, act rescissory), parliamentary composition, and the church's failure to protest as part of the justification for condemning the restoration and subsequent administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for ministers and societies to maintain covenantal purity (refuse corrupt associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faithful ministers must oppose public resolutions that admit 'malignant enemies' into places of power; societies should not join with parties whose membership includes known enemies to the work of reformation. Ministers who compromised (e.g., sent flattering addresses) are reproached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery praises ministers who refused association (e.g., those who opposed 1651 resolutions) and castigates those who took the King's toleration and sent addresses of thanks, labeling such behavior as betrayal of Presbyterian principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for reunion/communion: repentance, public confession, and purging of scandalous ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Before joining in communion with the national church, the Presbytery demanded humbling and acknowledgment of national sins, public confession and humiliation, and the purging of 'ignorant, insufficient, heterodox, and notoriously scandalous ministers' guilty of the blood of the saints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They submitted explicit paper proposals to the General Assembly (Edinburgh 1689-90) requesting these conditions; the proposals were rejected as 'unseasonable' by the majority. The Presbytery views such cleansing and confession as necessary for legitimate ecclesiastical communion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmation of and approbation for faithful testimony and martyrdom
rubrics_metrics.description: The Presbytery formally approves and homologates the testimony borne by witnesses and martyrs (from 1660 to the Revolution), who resisted public resolutions, stood by covenants, and suffered confiscation, imprisonment, banishment, and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document lists these sufferings as just grounds for approbation and holds up such faithfulness as the pattern ministers and people ought to follow when judging states and constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of the church to both vindicate faithful confessors and to denounce sin and wickedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The church's obligation is twofold: to bear witness unto the truth and justify Christ's confessors and martyrs, and to testify against sin and condemn the wicked for their wickedness, following precedents from the reformed and covenanted church of Scotland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural citations and historical precedent are invoked to support active denunciation of error and corruption, not merely passive remembrance of suffering.
